messages.content: What is the difference between positions and interests in negotiation?

Positions: what each party states they want. Interests: why they want it — the underlying need. Classic example (Fisher and Ury): two children fighting over an orange. Position vs position → split it in half. Interests: one wants the juice, one wants the peel for baking. Interests-based solution → one gets all the juice, one gets all the peel. Both are 100% satisfied vs 50% each. Moving from positions to interests: ask 'why is that important to you?' and 'what would that achieve?' Integrative solutions (expand the pie) are only visible at the level of interests.
What is BATNA and why is it the most important concept in negotiation?

BATNA: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. What you will do if this negotiation fails. Your BATNA determines your walk-away point and your actual leverage. If your BATNA is strong (you have other options), you negotiate from strength — you can genuinely walk away. If your BATNA is weak, you negotiate from desperation — the other party senses it and extracts concessions accordingly. Before any negotiation: strengthen your BATNA (develop alternatives), understand the other party's BATNA (what happens to them if this fails?). The zone of agreement exists only if both parties prefer the deal to their BATNA.
How do you negotiate salary effectively?

Never give the first number — whoever anchors first concedes psychological ground. If pressed: 'I'd like to understand the full scope of the role before discussing numbers.' Research: know market rates for your skills and location (Glassdoor, LinkedIn Salary, recruiter contacts). Know your BATNA: another offer or clear alternative vastly strengthens position. When you anchor: go higher than target with a specific rationale (not just 'I want more'). Odd specific numbers (£67,500) signal you've done research. Negotiate total compensation: base, bonus, equity, benefits, flexibility. Never accept on the spot — 'I need 24 hours to consider.'
What is tactical empathy in negotiation?

Tactical empathy (Chris Voss): understanding the other party's emotional state and perspective so thoroughly that you can articulate it better than they can. Not agreeing with them — understanding them. Technique: labelling ('It seems like you're frustrated that...') — labels the emotion without judging, invites confirmation or correction, builds rapport. Mirroring: repeat the last 2-3 words with a rising inflection — invites elaboration. People reveal more when they feel heard. The paradox: negotiators who focus most on understanding the other side get better outcomes than those focused on their own position.
What are the most common negotiation mistakes?

Anchoring too low: your first number sets the range — low anchor limits upside. Emotional reactivity: losing composure concedes leverage. Never let reaction reveal how much you want or fear something. Treating it as zero-sum: most negotiations have more variables than the obvious one — find value to exchange. Making concessions without extracting something: every concession without reciprocal movement signals your opening position was dishonest. Ignoring the relationship: in ongoing relationships, the negotiation outcome must leave the other party feeling fairly treated — winning at the expense of the relationship is costly long-term. Assuming you know their interests: ask more than you assume.
